title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: The temporary stable, a wooden shed, had been put up near the racecourse, and his mare was supposed to have been moved there the day before. He hadn't yet been to see her.

Over the last few days he hadn't ridden her out for exercise himself, but had left her in the trainer's hands, so right now he really had no idea what condition his mare had arrived in yesterday and was in today. He had barely stepped out of his carriage when his groom, the so-called "stable boy," recognizing the carriage from a distance, called for the trainer. A lean Englishman in tall boots and a short jacket, clean-shaven except for a tuft below his chin, came to meet him, walking with the awkward gait of a jockey, elbows turned outward and his body rocking from side to side.
"Well, how's Frou-Frou?" Vronsky asked in English.

"All right, sir," the Englishman's voice answered, somewhere down in his throat. "Better not go in," he added, touching his hat. "I've put a muzzle on her, and the mare's jumpy. Better not go in — it'll set her off."
"No, I'm going in. I want a look at her."
"Come along then," said the Englishman, frowning, speaking through closed lips, and with swinging elbows he led the way at his uneven gait.

They went into the small yard in front of the shed. A stable boy, smart and spruce in his holiday clothes, met them with a broom in hand and followed them in. In the shed there were five horses in separate stalls, and Vronsky knew that his chief rival, Gladiator, a very tall chestnut, had been brought here and must be standing among them. Even more than his own mare, Vronsky was longing to see Gladiator, whom he had never laid eyes on. But he knew that, by the etiquette of the racecourse, it was not only impossible for him to look at the horse but improper even to ask about him. As he was walking down the corridor, the boy opened the door to the second box on the left, and Vronsky caught a glimpse of a big chestnut horse with white legs. He knew this was Gladiator, but, with the feeling of a man turning his eyes away from another man's open letter, he turned and went into Frou-Frou's stall.
"The horse in here belongs to Mak... Mak... I can never get the name out," said the Englishman over his shoulder, jabbing his big finger with its dirty nail in the direction of Gladiator's stall.
"Mahotin? Yes — he's my most serious rival," said Vronsky.
"If you were riding him," the Englishman said, "I'd bet on you."
"Frou-Frou is more nervous; he is stronger," Vronsky said, smiling at the compliment to his riding.
"In a steeplechase, everything depends on the riding and on pluck," said the Englishman.

Of pluck — meaning energy and courage — Vronsky did not merely feel he had enough; what mattered far more, he was firmly convinced that no one in the world could possess more of this "pluck" than he did.
"You don't think I need to lose more weight?"

"Oh no," the Englishman answered. "Please don't speak loudly. The mare's jumpy," he added, nodding toward the horse-box, before which they were standing, and from which came the sound of restless stamping in the straw.

He opened the door, and Vronsky stepped into the horse-box, dimly lit by one small window. In the box stood a dark bay mare with a muzzle on, pawing at the fresh straw. Looking around him in the twilight of the box, Vronsky unconsciously took in once more, in a single sweeping glance, every point of his favorite mare. Frou-Frou was a beast of medium size, not entirely beyond reproach from a breeder's point of view. She was small-boned all over; though her chest was extremely prominent in front, it was narrow. Her hindquarters drooped a little, and in her forelegs, and still more in her hind legs, there was a noticeable bow. The muscles of both fore- and hind legs were not very heavy; but across her shoulders the mare was exceptionally broad — a feature especially striking now that she was lean from training. The bones of her legs below the knees looked, from the front, no thicker than a finger, but seen from the side they were extraordinarily thick. Apart from across her shoulders, she looked overall as though she had been pinched in at the sides and stretched out in depth. But she had, to the highest degree, the quality that makes one forget every fault: that quality was _blood_, the blood _that tells_, as the English expression puts it. Her muscles stood up sharply under the network of sinews, beneath a delicate, mobile skin soft as satin, and they were hard as bone. Her cleanly cut head, with its prominent, bright, spirited eyes, broadened at the open nostrils, which showed the red blood in the cartilage within. About her whole figure, and especially her head, there was a certain look of energy combined with softness. She was one of those creatures who seem unable to speak only because the structure of their mouths will not allow it.
To Vronsky, at any rate, it seemed that she understood everything he was feeling at that moment as he looked at her.

As soon as Vronsky stepped toward her she drew in a long breath and, rolling back her prominent eye until the white showed bloodshot, she shied at the approaching figures from the opposite side, shaking her muzzle and shifting lightly from one leg to the other.
"There — you see how jumpy she is," said the Englishman.
"There, my darling — there!" said Vronsky, going up to the mare and speaking soothingly to her.

But the closer he came, the more agitated she grew. Only when he was right at her head did she suddenly quiet, with the muscles trembling beneath her soft, delicate coat. Vronsky patted her strong neck, smoothed a stray lock of mane that had fallen on the wrong side of her sharp withers, and brought his face up close to her flared nostrils, sheer as a bat's wing. She drew a loud breath, snorted out through her tense nostrils, started, pricked her sharp ear, and stretched her strong black lip out toward Vronsky as if she wanted to nip his sleeve. Then, remembering the muzzle, she shook it, and once more began stamping restlessly with one shapely leg after another.
"Easy, my darling, easy!" he said, patting her again on the hindquarters; and, with the joyful sense that his mare was in the best possible condition, he stepped out of the box.
The mare's excitement had infected Vronsky. He felt his heart pounding, and he, too, like the mare, wanted to move, to bite; it was both dreadful and delicious.
"Well, I'm counting on you, then," he said to the Englishman; "half-past six on the ground."
"All right," said the Englishman. "Oh — where are you going, my lord?" he asked suddenly, using the title "my lord," which he had scarcely ever used before.

Vronsky raised his head in surprise and stared, in the way he knew how to stare — not into the Englishman's eyes but at his forehead — astonished at the impertinence of the question. But realizing that in asking it the Englishman had been speaking to him not as an employer but as a jockey, he answered:
"I've got to go to Bryansky's; I'll be home within an hour."

"That's the question I've been asked over and over today!" he said to himself, and he blushed — something that rarely happened to him. The Englishman looked gravely at him; and, as though he too knew where Vronsky was going, he added:
"The main thing's to stay calm before a race," he said. "Don't lose your temper, don't get worked up about anything."
"All right," Vronsky answered, smiling; and jumping into his carriage, he told the driver to head for Peterhof.
He had barely driven a few paces before the dark clouds that had been threatening rain all day broke, and a heavy downpour came down.

"What a shame!" thought Vronsky, putting up the roof of the carriage. "It was muddy before — now it'll be a perfect swamp." Alone in the closed carriage, he took out his mother's letter and his brother's note, and read them through.

Yes, it was the same thing all over again. Everyone — his mother, his brother, everyone — felt entitled to meddle in his heart's affairs. Their meddling stirred up in him a feeling of angry hatred — a feeling he had rarely known before. "What business is it of theirs? Why does everyone feel called on to make me his concern? And why do they have to badger me so? Just because they sense this is something they don't understand. If it were a common, vulgar, society intrigue, they would leave me alone. They feel this is something different, that this is not a mere amusement, that this woman is dearer to me than life. And that's incomprehensible to them, and that's why it makes them angry. Whatever our fate is or may be, we have made it ourselves, and we don't complain of it," he said, joining himself with Anna in the word _we_. "No, they have to teach us how to live. They have no idea what happiness is; they don't know that without our love, there is for us neither happiness nor unhappiness — no life at all," he thought.

He was angry with all of them for their meddling precisely because in his soul he felt that they — all these people — were right. He felt that the love that bound him to Anna was no momentary impulse that would pass, as society intrigues do pass, leaving in the life of either nothing more than pleasant or unpleasant memories. He felt all the torture of his own position and hers, all the difficulty of concealing their love when they were so conspicuous in the eyes of the world, of lying and deceiving — and of lying, deceiving, pretending, constantly thinking about other people, when the passion that bound them was so intense that they were both oblivious to anything but their love.

He pictured vividly all the constantly recurring instances when lying and deceit were forced on him — things so against his natural bent. He recalled particularly vividly the shame he had more than once seen in her at the necessity of such lying. And he had that strange feeling that had come over him several times since his secret love for Anna began. It was a feeling of loathing for something — whether for Alexey Alexandrovitch, or for himself, or for the world as a whole, he could not have said. But he always drove this strange feeling away. He shook it off now too, and picked up the thread of his thoughts.
"Yes — she was unhappy before, but proud and at peace; and now she cannot be at peace and feel secure in her dignity, though she does not show it. Yes, we have to put an end to this," he decided.

And for the first time the thought clearly took shape in him that it was essential to put an end to this false position, and the sooner the better. "Throw everything off, she and I, and hide ourselves somewhere alone with our love," he said to himself.
